meta.title: GRE Practice Test 1
meta.note: Original questions written for personal practice. Not ETS material.

essay.prompt: Governments should place greater emphasis on funding basic scientific research, which has no immediate practical purpose, than on research aimed at solving specific practical problems.
essay.instructions: Write a response in which you discuss how far you agree or disagree with this recommendation and explain the reasoning behind your position. As you develop your position, consider specific situations in which following the recommendation would and would not be beneficial, and explain how these situations shape your view.

guilds: For much of the twentieth century, historians treated the medieval guild primarily as an obstacle to economic growth.
Guilds, the argument ran, restricted entry into trades, fixed prices and suppressed innovation in order to protect the incomes of existing masters.
More recent scholarship has complicated this picture.
Several economic historians have pointed out that guilds also enforced quality standards, which allowed buyers in distant markets to trust goods they could not inspect in person.
Others have noted that guild apprenticeships provided a structured way of passing on skills at a time when few other forms of training existed.
None of these scholars claims that guilds were economically benign; rather, they argue that the institutions' effects varied with local circumstances and cannot be summarised by a single verdict.
predators: Some ecologists have proposed reintroducing large predators, such as wolves, to regions from which they were eliminated, on the grounds that predators regulate populations of grazing animals and thereby allow vegetation to recover.

Critics respond that the evidence for such cascading effects is drawn largely from a handful of well-publicised cases, and that in many landscapes human activity, rather than grazing, is the main constraint on plant growth.
In such places, they argue, reintroduced predators might reduce grazing without producing any visible recovery in vegetation.
bees: Honeybees communicate the location of food sources through a series of movements known as the waggle dance.
A forager returning to the hive moves in a straight line while shaking its body, then circles back to repeat the run.
The direction of the straight run, relative to vertical, indicates the direction of the food relative to the sun, while the duration of the run indicates the distance.
Researchers once assumed that other bees simply followed the dancer to the food.

Experiments in which dancers were tricked into misreporting distance, however, showed that recruits searched at the reported distance rather than the true one, demonstrating that they were decoding the dance itself.
bikes: Many cities have introduced bicycle-sharing schemes in the hope of reducing car traffic.
Surveys suggest, however, that most trips made on shared bicycles replace journeys that would otherwise have been made on foot or by public transport, not by car.

Supporters of the schemes argue that this finding understates their value, since the bicycles also make public transport more attractive by solving the problem of getting from a station to a final destination.
industry: The standard account of the Industrial Revolution emphasises technological invention: the steam engine, the spinning jenny and the power loom are presented as the engines of transformation.
Yet economic historians have long observed that many of these devices were known for decades before they were widely adopted.
Robert Allen has argued that the timing of adoption is better explained by relative prices.

In eighteenth-century Britain, wages were high and coal was cheap compared with continental Europe, so machines that substituted cheap energy for expensive labour were profitable there but not elsewhere.
On this view, invention was less a cause of industrialisation than a response to it: inventors directed their efforts toward the technologies that local conditions rewarded.

Critics have questioned whether British wages were in fact as high as Allen claims, but even they generally accept that the profitability of a technique, rather than its mere existence, determined how quickly it spread.
placebo: It is often said that the placebo effect demonstrates the power of belief over the body.

But many studies reporting large placebo effects lacked a no-treatment control group, so improvements attributed to the placebo may simply reflect the natural course of an illness or the tendency of extreme symptoms to become less extreme over time.
When trials include both a placebo group and an untreated group, the difference between them is often modest and confined to subjective outcomes, such as reported pain.

questions.stem: Although the novelist's early stories were dismissed as slight, her later work revealed a ______ that critics could no longer ignore: each book explored moral questions with growing depth.
questions.explain: The colon tells you the blank is explained by 'explored moral questions with growing depth', which means seriousness: gravity. 'Although ... slight' sets up the contrast.

questions.stem: The committee's report was notably ______; rather than taking a clear position, it presented every view as equally valid and recommended nothing.
questions.explain: Refusing to take a clear position is being equivocal (deliberately vague, non-committal). 'Incisive' and 'partisan' are the opposite.

questions.stem: The scientist was hardly a (i)______ of the new theory, which she had publicly called 'wishful thinking'; in fact, she had spent a decade gathering data that (ii)______ its central claim.
questions.explain: Calling the theory 'wishful thinking' shows she opposed it, so she was hardly a proponent (supporter), and her data undermined it.

questions.stem: Early accounts of the expedition portrayed its leader as (i)______, a man who never doubted his own judgement. Recently published letters, however, suggest a more (ii)______ figure, one who privately (iii)______ almost every major decision he made.
questions.explain: 'Never doubted his own judgement' = self-assured. 'However' signals the letters show the opposite: a conflicted man who agonised over his decisions.

questions.stem: Despite her reputation for being ______, the manager listened patiently to every complaint and rarely raised her voice.
questions.explain: 'Despite' means the reputation contrasts with patience and calm, so it must be bad temper: irascible and short-tempered mean the same thing.

questions.stem: The museum's new director, keen to make the collection less ______, removed the velvet ropes and invited visitors to touch selected objects.
questions.explain: Removing barriers and inviting touch makes a place less forbidding / intimidating. 'Accessible' is the opposite of what's needed.

questions.stem: Because the evidence was largely ______, the jury was instructed not to treat it as proof of guilt.
questions.explain: Evidence that cannot be treated as proof is circumstantial / indirect. 'Conclusive' and 'damning' point the wrong way.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
options: argue that guilds were beneficial to economic growth
describe a shift in how historians assess guilds
defend the twentieth-century view of guilds against its critics
compare guilds in different regions of Europe
questions.explain: The passage moves from the older 'obstacle' view to more recent, mixed assessments. It does not claim guilds were simply beneficial (the last sentence rules that out).

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following have recent scholars identified as functions of guilds? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Sentences 4 and 5 name quality standards and apprenticeships. Price-fixing is mentioned only as part of the older, negative view, and it would not lower prices.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which the author clarifies the limits of the recent scholars' position.
questions.explain: The last sentence says none of these scholars claims guilds were 'economically benign', which sets the limit of their claim.

questions.stem: The critics mentioned in the passage would most likely agree that
options: predators never affect populations of grazing animals
wolves should be removed from regions where they now live
vegetation recovery is caused mainly by human activity
the benefits of reintroducing predators may depend on local conditions
the well-publicised cases were based on fabricated data
questions.explain: The critics say that 'in many landscapes' other factors limit plant growth, so the benefit depends on the place. They never deny predators affect grazing.

questions.stem: In the context of the passage, 'constraint' most nearly means
questions.explain: Human activity is the main thing limiting plant growth, so 'constraint' means limitation.

questions.stem: The instructions were so ______ that even first-time users assembled the shelf without difficulty.
questions.explain: Easy assembly means the instructions were clear: lucid.

questions.stem: Rather than ______ the mistake, the company admitted it publicly and offered refunds.
questions.explain: 'Rather than' contrasts with admitting publicly, so the blank is hiding it: concealing.

questions.stem: Critics found the film's plot ______: every twist could be seen coming long before it arrived.
questions.explain: The colon explains the blank: twists seen coming = predictable.

questions.stem: The town's population, once (i)______, has (ii)______ steadily since the factory closed, and many houses now stand empty.
questions.explain: Empty houses show the population declined; 'once' signals it used to be the opposite: thriving.

questions.stem: Although the speech was (i)______, lasting barely five minutes, it was far from (ii)______; listeners remembered its key arguments for years.
questions.explain: 'Barely five minutes' = brief. Remembered for years = far from forgettable.

questions.stem: The new policy was meant to (i)______ congestion in the city centre, but by making parking cheaper it actually (ii)______ more drivers, and traffic grew (iii)______.
questions.explain: 'Meant to ... but ... actually' signals the policy backfired: meant to ease congestion, but cheaper parking attracted drivers and traffic grew heavier.

questions.stem: The professor was known for her ______ lectures, which students found difficult to sit through.
questions.explain: Hard to sit through = boring: tedious and wearisome.

questions.stem: The hikers were ______ after the long climb and rested for an hour before continuing.
questions.explain: Resting after a long climb implies tiredness: exhausted and fatigued. 'Hungry' may fit the sentence but has no matching synonym.

questions.stem: Though the plan seemed ______ at first, it proved to be entirely practical.
questions.explain: 'Though' contrasts with 'practical', so the plan seemed impractical: fanciful and unrealistic.

questions.stem: The diplomat's ______ remarks helped calm an otherwise tense meeting.
questions.explain: Remarks that calm tension are conciliatory (peace-making) and soothing.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with
options: describing how honeybees signal the location of food and how other bees use that signal
comparing honeybees with other insects that live in colonies
arguing that bees cannot perceive the position of the sun
explaining why bees perform the waggle dance only at night
criticising the experimental methods of early bee researchers
questions.explain: The passage describes the dance, then reports experiments showing recruits decode it. The other options are not discussed.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the duration of the straight run indicates the
questions.explain: Sentence 3: 'the duration of the run indicates the distance'.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred about the experiments described in the final sentence? Select all that apply.
options: They showed that recruits relied on information contained in the dance.
They contradicted an assumption that researchers had previously held.
They proved that bees cannot locate food by smell.
questions.explain: Recruits searched where the dance said, so they used the dance, which contradicts the earlier 'just follow the dancer' assumption. Smell is never mentioned.

questions.stem: The surveys mentioned in the passage suggest that bicycle-sharing schemes
options: mostly replace trips that would have been made on foot or by public transport
cost more to run than public transport
questions.explain: Sentence 2 says exactly this.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that presents a response to the survey findings.
questions.explain: The third sentence gives the supporters' reply: the findings understate the schemes' value.

questions.stem: Far from being ______, the historian's prose is so dense with qualification that readers often lose track of her argument.
questions.explain: 'Far from being' needs the opposite of dense and hard to follow: limpid (perfectly clear). The other options all describe difficult prose.

questions.stem: The senator's reputation for ______ was undone when reporters revealed that he had quietly accepted gifts from the very industry he claimed to regulate.
questions.explain: Taking gifts destroys a reputation for honesty: probity. 'Venality' (corruptibility) is the opposite.

questions.stem: Her praise was so carefully ______, with every compliment paired with a reservation, that colleagues wondered whether it was praise at all.
questions.explain: Compliments paired with reservations = hedged (qualified).

questions.stem: The theory's (i)______ is also its weakness: because it can accommodate any possible outcome, it makes no predictions that could ever be (ii)______.
questions.explain: Accommodating any outcome = flexibility. A theory that fits every outcome can never be shown wrong: falsified.

questions.stem: Scholars once regarded the poet's late works as (i)______, the hasty products of a mind in decline; yet a closer reading reveals a deliberate (ii)______, a stripping away of ornament in pursuit of clarity.
questions.explain: 'Hasty products' = slapdash (careless). 'Stripping away of ornament' = austerity (plainness).

questions.stem: The author's argument (i)______ correlation with causation, an error she never (ii)______; consequently, her conclusions, though (iii)______, rest on shaky foundations.
questions.explain: Treating correlation as causation = conflates. She never acknowledges the error. 'Though' needs a strength that contrasts with 'shaky foundations': her conclusions are persuasive on the surface but poorly grounded.

questions.stem: The critic's review was unusually ______, dismissing the novel in a single contemptuous paragraph.
questions.explain: One quick paragraph = perfunctory / cursory (done with minimal effort).

questions.stem: Though outwardly ______, the negotiator was privately convinced that the talks would fail.
questions.explain: 'Though' contrasts with privately expecting failure, so outwardly hopeful: sanguine and optimistic.

questions.stem: The ______ of the evidence surprised investigators, who had expected the records to be patchy and contradictory.
questions.explain: The surprise is the opposite of 'contradictory': coherence and consistency. 'Abundance' answers only 'patchy' and has no synonym among the options.

questions.stem: Rather than resolving the dispute, the court's ruling merely ______ it, prompting both sides to file fresh appeals.
questions.explain: Fresh appeals from both sides show the dispute got worse: exacerbated / aggravated.

questions.stem: The author mentions that many devices 'were known for decades before they were widely adopted' primarily in order to
options: suggest that invention alone does not explain when industrialisation occurred
praise the foresight of early inventors
show that the standard account is entirely mistaken
argue that British wages were lower than claimed
show that British inventors copied European designs
questions.explain: The delay between invention and adoption undercuts the idea that invention drove the timing, setting up Allen's price explanation. 'Entirely mistaken' goes too far.

questions.stem: Allen's argument, as described in the passage, would predict which of the following? Select all that apply.
options: A labour-saving machine would be adopted more quickly where wages are high.
Inventors would focus on technologies that local prices made profitable.
Countries with expensive coal would be the first to adopt coal-powered machines.
questions.explain: High wages make labour-saving profitable (A), and inventors respond to what local conditions reward (B). Expensive coal would discourage coal-powered machines, so C is the reverse.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that identifies a point on which Allen and his critics agree.
questions.explain: The last sentence: 'even they generally accept' that profitability determined the spread of a technique.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the claim made in the first sentence is best described as
questions.explain: The author doubts the claim because of flawed study design, but admits a modest effect on subjective outcomes: sceptical, but with qualifications.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's argument?
options: Patients given placebos often report reduced pain.
Placebos are cheaper to produce than active drugs.
In a trial with both a placebo group and an untreated group, the two groups showed similar improvement in objectively measured blood pressure.
Patients who believe in a treatment are more likely to take it regularly.
questions.explain: The author argues that properly controlled trials show little placebo effect on objective outcomes. Option D is exactly such evidence. Option A supports the opposite view.
Cross-multiply (both denominators are positive): compare x(x + 2) = x² + 2x with (x + 1)² = x² + 2x + 1. B is always larger by 1.
4⁵ = (2²)⁵ = 2¹⁰. They are equal.

questions.given: n is an integer and 3 < n < 6.
questions.explain: n could be 4 (B bigger) or 5 (A bigger), so the relationship cannot be determined.
Area = 9π ≈ 28.27, which is less than 28.5.

questions.stem: A shirt priced at $40 is discounted by 25%. The discounted price is then increased by 20%. What is the final price?
questions.explain: $40 × 0.75 = $30; $30 × 1.20 = $36. Percentage changes do not cancel out.

questions.stem: If 3x − 7 = 2x + 5, what is the value of x?
questions.explain: Subtract 2x from both sides: x − 7 = 5, so x = 12.

questions.stem: The average (arithmetic mean) of five numbers is 18. If one of the numbers, 30, is removed, what is the average of the remaining four numbers?
Which of the following are factors of 84? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: 84 = 2² × 3 × 7. 6, 12, 14 and 21 divide it. 8 needs 2³ and 24 needs 2³ × 3, so neither does.

questions.stem: A right triangle has legs of length 6 and 8. What is its perimeter?
questions.explain: Hypotenuse = √(36 + 64) = 10. Perimeter = 6 + 8 + 10 = 24.

questions.stem: A bag holds 4 red and 6 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are red? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.explain: 4/10 × 3/9 = 12/90 = 2/15. Any equivalent fraction is accepted.

questions.stem: By what percent did non-fiction sales increase from 2023 to 2024?
questions.explain: Increase = 30 − 25 = 5. 5 ÷ 25 = 0.20 = 20%. (16.7% would be 5 ÷ 30, the wrong base.)

questions.stem: In 2024, which categories accounted for more than 25% of total sales? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Total is 100, so shares are 46%, 30%, 12% and 12%. Only fiction and non-fiction exceed 25%.
Both equal 20.
x² = 9 and 2x = −6.

questions.qa: The number of minutes in 3 hours
questions.qb: The number of seconds in 4 minutes
questions.explain: 3 × 60 = 180 minutes; 4 × 60 = 240 seconds.
If y = 2, B is bigger; if y = 0.5, A is bigger; if y = 1 they're equal. Cannot be determined.

questions.stem: What is 15% of 80?
If 5x + 4 = 29, what is the value of x?
A rectangle has length 12 cm and width 5 cm. What is the length of its diagonal, in centimetres?
In a class of 40 students, the ratio of boys to girls is 3 : 5. How many girls are in the class?
questions.explain: 3 + 5 = 8 parts; each part = 40 ÷ 8 = 5 students. Girls = 5 × 5 = 25.

questions.stem: Which of the following numbers are prime? Select all that apply.
A car travels 150 km in 2.5 hours. What is its average speed, in kilometres per hour?
If a = 2 and b = −3, what is the value of a² − ab?
What is 1/3 + 1/4? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.explain: Common denominator 12: 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12.

questions.stem: What is the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon (a six-sided polygon)?
If x² = 16, which of the following could be the value of x? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Both 4² and (−4)² equal 16.

questions.stem: What is the median of the numbers 3, 9, 4, 7, 12 and 5?
questions.explain: In order: 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 12. With six numbers the median is the average of the middle two: (5 + 7) ÷ 2 = 6.

questions.given: x and y are positive and x > y.
questions.explain: (x + y)/2 − √(xy) = (√x − √y)²/2, which is positive whenever x ≠ y. So A is always greater.

questions.qa: The number of positive divisors of 36
questions.qb: The number of positive divisors of 48

questions.given: k is an integer and k² < 20.
questions.explain: k can be any integer from −4 to 4. If k = 4 they are equal; if k = 3, B is bigger. Cannot be determined.
Multiply A top and bottom by (√3 − √2): denominator becomes 3 − 2 = 1, so A = √3 − √2.

questions.stem: In a club, 60% of members are women. 25% of the women and 40% of the men wear glasses. What percent of all members wear glasses?
questions.explain: 0.60 × 0.25 = 0.15 and 0.40 × 0.40 = 0.16. Total 0.31 = 31%. (32.5% is the trap of simply averaging 25% and 40%.)

questions.stem: In how many different ways can a committee of 3 people be chosen from a group of 8?
questions.explain: Order does not matter: 8C3 = (8 × 7 × 6) ÷ (3 × 2 × 1) = 56.

questions.stem: If 2^(x + 3) = 32^(x − 1), what is the value of x?
If n is an odd integer, which of the following must be true? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Odd² is odd, so n² + 1 is even. n + 1 is even, so n(n + 1) is even. n² − 1 = (n − 1)(n + 1), the product of two consecutive even numbers, one of which is a multiple of 4, so it's divisible by 8. 3n is odd. With n = 1, (n + 3)/2 = 2, which is even.

questions.stem: A circle is inscribed in a square with side length 10. What is the area of the region inside the square but outside the circle?
questions.explain: The circle's diameter equals the side, so radius = 5 and its area = 25π. Square area = 100. Difference = 100 − 25π.

questions.stem: An arithmetic sequence has first term 7 and common difference 4. What is the sum of its first 20 terms?
A fair six-sided die is rolled twice. What is the probability that the two results add up to 8? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.explain: Pairs: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2), which is 5 of the 36 equally likely outcomes.

questions.stem: Pipe A can fill a tank in 6 hours. Pipe B can empty the full tank in 9 hours. If the tank starts empty and both pipes are open, how many hours will it take to fill the tank?
questions.explain: Net rate = 1/6 − 1/9 = 3/18 − 2/18 = 1/18 of the tank per hour, so 18 hours.

questions.stem: Approximately what percent of all employees work remotely?
In which departments do more than 40% of employees work remotely? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: Sales 32/80 = exactly 40% (not more than). Engineering 84/120 = 70%. Finance 9/36 = 25%. Support 45/84 ≈ 53.6%.

questions.stem: If 15 Engineering employees switch from remote to office work, what percent of Engineering employees will then work in the office? (Enter the number only.)
